strengths: Significant theoretical contribution: O(d log d) finite regret bound for M-convex sets substantially improves over prior O(d log T) results, partially resolving an open question

Elegant technical approach: Creative synthesis of M-convex structural characterization (Proposition 2.4) with geometric volume arguments (Lemma 4.1, Grünbaum's theorem) is both novel and well-executed
Novel corruption detection: Graph acyclicity-based corruption handling (Lemmas 5.1-5.2) is clever, adaptive, and does not require knowing C in advance
Rigorous mathematical analysis: Proofs appear sound with careful handling of technical details; includes matching lower bound (up to log d factor)
Well-motivated setting: Clear justification for M-convex action sets with concrete examples (matroids, integer lattice extensions); good pedagogical progression from O(d²) to O(d log d) algorithm
Complete treatment: Addresses both uncorrupted and corrupted feedback; comprehensive problem setup and clear presentation overall
weaknesses: Restricted scope limits impact: Only partially resolves the open question by restricting to M-convex sets; the main question asked about polynomial bounds for general action sets, limiting practical applicability
Critical lack of experimental validation: No experiments, empirical verification, baseline comparisons, or computational time measurements; concerning absence for an algorithmic paper

Unresolved computational complexity: Center of gravity computation is #P-hard requiring randomized LV algorithm with O(n⁴) complexity; per-round costs not thoroughly analyzed or compared to alternatives
Loose log d gap: O(d log d) upper bound vs. Ω(d) lower bound; gap is not closed and no analysis of whether it is fundamental
Limited corruption model: Only handles adversarial corruptions up to C rounds; cannot handle cumulative suboptimality framework from Sakaue et al. (2025b), deferring to future work
Incomplete practical guidance: No discussion of how algorithm scales with very large d, parameter tuning, or whether center of gravity computation is practically viable in practice
Assumption 2.2 restrictions: Requires per-round regret O(1) and distinct w* components, somewhat limiting generality
Lower bound construction concerns: Requires embedding into d+1 dimensions; unclear if construction is optimal or if log d gap can be closed

strengths: Solves part of an open problem: achieves O(d log d) finite regret bound for M-convex sets, improving over prior O(d log T) or exp(O(d log d)) bounds
Technically sound core contributions: clever combination of M-convexity's exchange property (Prop. 2.4) with Grünbaum's volume argument and order simplex decomposition
Novel corruption detection via directed graph acyclicity: corruption-robust bound O((C+1)d log d) without knowing C is creative and practical
Complete picture: provides upper bound O(d log d), lower bound Ω(d), showing tightness up to log d factor
Well-presented progression: warm-up O(d²) algorithm provides good intuition before refined O(d log d) algorithm
Broad applicability within M-convex class: includes matroids and natural extensions to integer lattice problems
weaknesses: Restricted scope limits impact: improvements apply only to M-convex sets, a narrow subclass of combinatorial optimization problems; applicability to general polyhedral or convex sets remains unclear
Unresolved O(log d) gap: no intuition for why volume argument doesn't close the gap to Ω(d) lower bound, leaving question of whether gap is fundamental or technical artifact

Critical computational complexity not addressed: center-of-gravity computation (Step 3) requires randomized polynomial-time approximation, but Theorem 4.2 analysis assumes exact computation; approximation error bounds should be explicit in main results, not buried in time complexity discussion
Assumption 2.2 is restrictive and somewhat artificial: distinct components of w* requires perturbation arguments that add technical baggage; O(1) per-round regret hides structure of feasible sets

No empirical validation: purely theoretical paper with no experiments, making practical relevance unclear; synthetic experiments on matroids (e.g., matchings, graphic matroids) would strengthen claims

Limited novelty in individual components: volume argument borrowed from contextual pricing literature (Liu et al. 2021), M-convexity from Murota (2003), restart mechanism inspired by Gupta et al. (2025); originality is primarily in the combination

Insufficient motivation for M-convexity: while well-written, the argument that M-convex sets are special (curved sets trivial, general polyhedral hard, M-convex has structure) is somewhat hand-wavy; practical applications remain unclear without examples

Incomplete analysis of corruptions: paper uses standard corruption model but acknowledges Sakaue et al.'s cumulative suboptimality is more flexible; extension to this model left as future work, limiting contribution

strengths: Resolves (partially) important open question: achieves O(d log d) finite regret bound, removing problematic T-dependence from prior O(d log T) bounds and exponential dependence from exp(O(d log d))
Technically sound and elegant: combines M-convex characterization (Proposition 2.4) with geometric volume arguments via Grünbaum's theorem; all proofs are rigorous and correct
Comprehensive theoretical treatment: provides both O(d log d) upper bound and matching Ω(d) lower bound (tight up to log d factor), giving strong theoretical guarantees
Creative corruption-robust extension: adaptive detection via directed graph acyclicity elegantly identifies corruptions without requiring prior knowledge of C; achieves O((C+1)d log d)
Well-motivated problem setting: M-convex action sets include matroids and natural extensions, balancing practical relevance with sufficient structure for improved bounds

Clear presentation with good pedagogical structure: O(d²) warm-up algorithm builds intuition before refinement to O(d log d); helpful examples and figures (especially Figure 2); problem formulation well-justified (Remark 2.1)
weaknesses: Limited scope: results restricted to M-convex action sets; unclear whether similar techniques apply to non-M-convex polyhedral or smooth convex sets, limiting applicability
Remaining theoretical gap: O(log d) gap between O(d log d) upper bound and Ω(d) lower bound not closed; no discussion of whether gap is fundamental or technique-limited
Computational practicality concerns: center of gravity computation is #P-hard and requires randomized approximation; impact of approximation error on regret bounds not rigorously analyzed
No experimental validation: paper is purely theoretical; even synthetic experiments comparing O(d²) vs O(d log d) algorithms or validating corruption detection would strengthen contributions

Presentation issues: duplicate Figure 1 (pages 8-9), notation switching between A_t and A_{t':t+1} is confusing, M-convexity background may be dense for readers unfamiliar with discrete convex analysis
Artificial technical assumption: Assumption 2.2 condition 2 (distinct components of w*) requires perturbation argument; deeper discussion of how ties manifest in practice would improve clarity

strengths: Significant theoretical contribution: achieves O(d log d) regret for M-convex action sets, partially resolving open question about polynomial (in d) finite regret bounds independent of T
Novel technical approach combining M-convex structure characterization (Proposition 2.4) with geometric volume argument (Grünbaum's theorem) and graph-theoretic corruption detection (acyclicity)
Comprehensive treatment including warm-up O(d²) algorithm, refined O(d log d) algorithm, corruption robustness without prior knowledge of C, and matching Ω(d) lower bound (tight up to log d)
Well-motivated problem class: M-convex sets encompass matroids and extensions, forming natural subclass of polyhedral combinatorial structures
Sound technical development with rigorous proofs; lower bound construction via M♮-convex embedding is non-trivial
Honest treatment of limitations and assumptions; thorough appendices on implementation details, computational complexity, and edge cases
weaknesses: Computational complexity is prohibitive: O(d log d)-regret algorithm requires Õ(d⁶ log d · log T) per-round time via approximate center of gravity, making it impractical despite theoretical improvements. Table 2 shows 1.1ms per round for d=20

Very limited experimental validation: single synthetic experiment on d=20 uniform matroids; no real applications or problem instances; ONS baseline achieves similar regret to O(d²) version, not strongly validating the M-convex approach
O(log d) gap between upper and lower bounds remains unresolved, suggesting bound may not be tight and raising questions about the true complexity

Restriction to M-convex sets limits applicability; no empirical data on prevalence of M-convexity in real inverse optimization problems; paper acknowledges many important settings violate this assumption

Corruption model requires distinct components of w* (Assumption 2.2) for detection mechanism; while removable in uncorrupted case, corrupted case remains limited; differs from cumulative suboptimality model (acknowledged as future work)

Approximate center of gravity implementation adds substantial technical complexity (approximate Grünbaum theorem, union bounds over T) that detracts from clarity; practical tuning of τ, δ parameters underdiscussed

Limited novelty in individual technical components (Grünbaum's theorem is classical; volume-based analysis standard in online learning; hit-and-run known); novelty primarily in combination for this problem

For ICML venue: primarily theoretical contribution with minimal practical validation; high computational costs and single toy-scale experiment insufficient for demonstrating practical utility; stronger fits would be theory venues like COLT
